key_points.point_text: Central thesis: outcome differences trace to proposing versus receiving, not talent, luck, or choice quality.
key_points.evidence_quote: "nothing to do with talent, luck, or even the quality of their choices" (1)
key_points.reasoning: Thesis restated with all three exclusions and the propose/receive distinction intact.

key_points.point_text: The 1962 Gale-Shapley setup: proving stable matchings always exist and presenting an algorithm to find them.
key_points.evidence_quote: "In 1962, David Gale and Lloyd Shapley worked on creating stable pairings" (1.2)
key_points.reasoning: Year, names, stability goal, existence proof, and algorithm all captured.

key_points.point_text: Deferred acceptance result: proposers get their best stable partner, receivers their worst, provably extreme for each individual.
key_points.evidence_quote: "Proposers get their best possible partner among all stable matchings, while receivers get their worst" (1.5)
key_points.reasoning: Mechanism, best/worst asymmetry, and extremity nuance all present with exact scope.

key_points.point_text: Real-world systems share the proposer-receiver structure even roughly, so the same pattern is expected.
key_points.evidence_quote: "they share the structure: one side initiates, the other responds" (2.2)
key_points.reasoning: The not-exact-algorithm caveat and "even roughly" scope survive in the theme.

key_points.point_text: Everyday examples (Netflix, phone, job, friendship) show that most of us default to receiving.
key_points.evidence_quote: "For most of these, most of us are receivers" (3.5)
key_points.reasoning: All four examples and both "most" hedges preserved.

key_points.point_text: Receiver outcomes are acceptable and good enough but not best, and the system is self-sustaining because it never stings enough to prompt revolt; you never know what you are missing.
key_points.evidence_quote: "does not screw you badly enough to make you revolt" (3.9); "You do not even know what you are missing" (3.10)
key_points.reasoning: The terrible-outcomes negation, decent-vs-best distinction, no-conspiracy note, and stability mechanism all preserved.

key_points.point_text: The chicken-and-egg trap: intention is needed to propose but develops only through proposing, and selecting among presented options reveals only the least-disliked choice.
key_points.evidence_quote: "you need intention to propose, but you develop intention through proposing" (4.3)
key_points.reasoning: Trap, least-disliked mechanism, and the lost/never-developed capacity all captured.

key_points.point_text: The intention muscle builds progressively: start small tonight, and patterns become preferences then values, since values are practiced into, not thought into.
key_points.evidence_quote: "Start tonight: before opening any app, decide what you actually want" (5.2); "practice your way into them" (5.6)
key_points.reasoning: Progressive-build claim, the small start, the values chain, and the think/practice negation all present.

key_points.point_text: Major life decisions also run on presented options, and proposers end up systematically better off, not smarter or luckier.
key_points.evidence_quote: "Most people, most of the time, are evaluating presented options" (6.3); "Not because they are smarter or luckier" (6.7)
key_points.reasoning: Receiver default, feels-like-agency nuance, proposer behaviors, and the not-smarter/luckier negation preserved.

key_points.point_text: Collective effect: systems optimize for whoever proposes, the platforms are the proposers, they collect attention, data, and money, and you stay because leaving is harder.
key_points.evidence_quote: "The proposers in these systems are not the users; they are the platforms" (7.4)
key_points.reasoning: All three platform examples, the platform-as-proposer claim, and the stability-persistence mechanism present.

key_points.point_text: Understanding does not remove the disadvantage; you must switch positions, and proposing means deciding before seeing, pursuing specifics, creating opportunities, and accepting friction.
key_points.evidence_quote: "Understanding the disadvantage does not remove it" (8); "deciding intentionally what you want before seeing what is available" (8.2)
key_points.reasoning: All four definitional bullets, the every-major/most-minor scope, and the designed-environment claim captured.

key_points.point_text: Most people will not make the shift (it is effortful and comfortable), but those who do get structurally, not incrementally, better outcomes.
key_points.evidence_quote: "Most people will not do this" (8.7); "Systematically better, not just incrementally: structurally" (8.10)
key_points.reasoning: Refusal reasons, the not-exact-mathematics caveat, and the structural (not incremental) emphasis preserved.

key_points.point_text: The closing challenge: the dynamic is confirmed by mathematics and observed patterns, and the open question is whether the reader will act.
key_points.evidence_quote: "The question is whether you are willing to do something about it" (8.12)

key_points.point_text: Appendix drills: three-week entertainment plan, shopping rules (3-5 features, $100 day, toothpaste), career quarter (two-week energy map, 5 non-negotiables, 4-of-5), relationships (3-5 values), micro-practices (three intentions, 10-second pause), and a 30-day three-column journal.
key_points.evidence_quote: "For anything over $100, wait a day after deciding" (10.2.5); "After 30 days the pattern is clear" (10.6.4)
key_points.reasoning: Every exercise and numeric rule from the appendix is present; $100, 3-5, 4-of-5, 10 seconds, and 30 days all survive.

key_points.point_text: Key insight: intention is not about knowing everything, it is practicing the question "what do I want?" before someone else answers, starting small until it becomes natural.
key_points.evidence_quote: "practicing the question what do I want before someone else provides the answer" (10.8)
key_points.reasoning: The negation, the practice framing, and the progressive-growth close all present.
